item.title: Do bioacoustic foundation models hear through the noise ? SNR and generalization in underwater detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.33068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bioacoustic foundation models are claimed to generalize across taxa and recording conditions, but are trained mainly on terrestrial archives of focal, high-quality recordings and evaluated on benchmarks emphasizing architecture over data conditions. We evaluate four such models as frozen encoders on an underwater detection task, using linear probing on continuously recorded data from the Kerguelen Plateau. Four datasets of identical size were built to differ only in the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of their positive segments, and probes were trained and evaluated across all combinations. Evaluation SNR accounts for more variation in average precision (AP) than model choice, and performance peaks when training and evaluation share a noise regime --- the configuration least representative of a continuous deployment. Training on mixed SNR redistributes performance toward low-SNR conditions without improving it overall, and AP remains low throughout. In light of these results, we call for evaluation standards grounded in realistic noise and deployment conditions rather than curated, high-quality recordings.
item.dc:creator: Lucie Jean-Labadye, Nicolas Farrugia, Axel Marmoret, Dorian Cazau, Olivier Adam

item.title: Measuring Local Acoustic Contribution in Speech LLMs via Word-Span Counterfactual Interventions
item.description: arXiv:2610.33077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Correct transcription does not establish that a word depended on its local audio. We introduce the Acoustic Evidence Contribution (AEC), a word-level counterfactual measure of acoustic grounding. It is obtained from the change in reference-token log likelihood when the word's aligned acoustic span is replaced. We combine decoding outcomes on unedited audio with thresholded AEC in an outcome-contribution matrix, where correct targets are categorized according to their local acoustic contribution as high or low. Depending on the system, 33-49% of correct single-word targets fall below the twofold contribution threshold when averaged across corpora, despite no evident rank association with WER. Retention of reference words after span removal decreases monotonically across AEC quintiles, from 76-83% in the lowest quintile to approximately 1% in the highest. AEC therefore separates transcription correctness from dependence on the aligned local acoustic span while remaining an oracle-aligned diagnostic method.
item.dc:creator: Hardik B. Sailor, Qiongqiong Wang, Dheemant Rastogi, Nancy F. Chen, Ai Ti Aw

item.title: MarineSet: Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Data Curation and evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The scarcity of labeled underwater acoustic data limits the development of data-driven models for marine acoustic monitoring, motivating the use of self-supervised learning to exploit the abundance of unlabeled recordings. However, large-scale data alone does not guarantee effective representation learning, because model performance is strongly influenced by the distribution of the training data. To facilitate such training data, this study introduces a scalable curation pipeline that curates 3,000 hours from 41 years of raw NOAA hydrophone recordings, producing MarineSet, a large-scale and diverse dataset designed for underwater acoustic learning. A baseline model, MarineNet, trained on MarineSet achieves competitive performance on marine mammal call and ship-type classification, highlighting the value of systematic data curation for developing self-supervised learning models in underwater acoustics.
item.dc:creator: Hilde I. Hummel, Sandjai Bhulai, Rob D. van der Mei, Burooj Ghani

item.title: JIT-MPE: Just-in-Time Multi-Pitch Estimation under Output Deadlines
item.description: arXiv:2610.33113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Live pitch displays, score followers and accompaniment systems must know which pitches are sounding within tens of milliseconds, but instrument-agnostic multi-pitch estimation (MPE) has mainly been designed and evaluated offline. We present JIT-MPE, a causal MPE model of 86k parameters for mixed ensembles. It gives an immediate estimate of each 20 ms frame and re-estimates the same frame as 20, 40, 80 and 160 ms of further audio arrive, so that a live display can show pitches at once and then refine them. We score each output only at a deadline by which it can be computed from the audio that has arrived, on five development sets and four held-out sets evaluated only after all design choices were frozen. At a 50 ms deadline, which reads the update made with 40 ms of lookahead, JIT-MPE is significantly more accurate than five of six published offline MPE systems in 38 of 45 comparisons (15 of 20 on the held-out sets) and less accurate in only two, although these systems read the whole recording and all but one have 6 to 170 times as many parameters; the sixth, supervised on URMP, is higher on four of the nine sets. The deadline costs little: on the held-out sets, JIT-MPE at 50 ms is within $-1.27$ to $+0.60$ points of recording-level macro F1 of its own final output with 160 ms of lookahead and within $-2.08$ to $+0.79$ points of a bidirectional model of similar size. Waiting pays off where the immediate estimate is weakest: the update at 50 ms adds 1.7-3.6 points over it on the development data and three of the four held-out sets, and raises the recall of reference frames in the first 20 ms after a note onset from 9.8% to 38.4% on the held-out AAM set. The slowest measured frame takes at most 4.15 ms on one CPU thread. Code and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Frieve-A/jit-mpe.
item.dc:creator: Yoshiyuki Kobayashi

item.title: Beyond Visible Speakers: Context-Aware Active Speaker Detection with Speaker Registration
item.description: arXiv:2610.33127v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.
item.dc:creator: Pu Wang, Hugo Van hamme

item.title: DJustify: Reason-and-Verify DJ Planning for Pop Transitions and Story-Driven Sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.33434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic DJ systems mostly target electronic dance music, whose regular structure makes rule-based mixing relatively easier. Vocal-rich popular music is harder: which track to play next, where to cue it, and which transition to use are tied together, so fixed rules handle them poorly. We present DJustify, a pop AI-DJ that puts an LLM in a reason--propose--verify--repair loop and lets it choose the next track, cue points, and mixing technique together. The LLM samples several transition plans; an external acoustic checker then scores the rendered audio and triggers repair when a check fails. Sampling keeps several candidate transitions per track pair instead of one fixed mix. In blind listening tests our transitions beat Mosaikbox, a reimplemented crossfade, and a cue baseline that reuses the crossfade's cues; that last comparison shows most of the margin comes from cue placement. The same planner also picks and orders a set along an emotion arc: this improves story coherence over a no-story ablation, and within a set story and transition ratings show no measurable gap from a human DJ. The checker mainly adds reliability, not higher average quality: it repairs rare but audible errors such as cut vocals, while the planner stays non-deterministic.
item.dc:creator: Wei-Han Hsu, Li-Jie Lin, Po-Hsuan Lai, Po-Hsiang Huang, Jeng-Yue Liu, Li Su, Yi-Hsuan Yang

item.title: Music of the Deep: An acoustic blueprint of sperm whale codas
item.description: arXiv:2610.33974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sperm-whale codas are usually described by the number and timing of their clicks. Earlier acoustic studies showed that individual clicks and longer coda sequences contain additional organization. We ask how that organization compares with music, whose smaller sounds also form larger units and ordered sequences. We compare codas with performed violin music, drum grooves, and sung melodies. Their sequences resemble music in some measures of predictability, yet codas show a different relationship between the smaller sounds within a unit and the order of units across a sequence. This combination was not observed in the musical references tested. Coda timing also varies coherently and carries information about individual callers. The recordings show another striking property: broad, reproducible variation along acoustic dimensions associated with human ratings of emotion, with a range comparable to human audio in most eligible tests. These findings motivate an acoustic blueprint that describes natural codas beyond their click timing. Its importance is apparent in synthetic audio: WhAM produces recognizable coda-like recordings, yet the tested clips remain distinguishable from natural codas in five of six acoustic comparisons after strict matching. The blueprint provides a fuller way to study natural codas and to evaluate how faithfully synthetic recordings represent them.
item.dc:creator: Mudit Sinha, Sanika Chavan

item.title: EmoNet: A Lightweight Attention-Based CNN for Speech Emotion Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2610.33977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) is a fundamental task in affective computing that enables applications such as mental health assessment, human-computer interaction, and automated customer support systems. Accurate emotion classification from speech remains challenging due to variations in speaker style, acoustic conditions, and the high computational cost of modern deep learning approaches. Many existing systems depend on large transformer-based architectures that require substantial computational resources, making them less suitable for real-time or resource-constrained environments. This research proposes EmoNet, a lightweight deep learning framework for speech emotion classification across seven emotion categories. The model is built on a four-block depthwise separable CNN encoder with squeeze-and-excitation attention and residual connections, combined with a Bidirectional LSTM for temporal feature learning and a multi-head attention pooling mechanism for improved representation. A comprehensive 134-channel acoustic feature set alongside data augmentation techniques including audio-level perturbations and SpecAugment is employed to improve robustness under diverse acoustic conditions. Evaluated on a combined dataset of TESS, RAVDESS, and SAVEE, EmoNet achieves a test accuracy of 96.75% with only 4.11 million parameters. The proposed model outperforms its reproduced baseline and remains competitive with significantly larger state-of-the-art architectures.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Moiz Khalid, Abdur Rehman Tariq, Muhammad Okasha Yamin

item.title: ASR-Protected Fusion and Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization for Joint ASR and Word-Level Speech Anti-Spoofing
item.description: arXiv:2610.34156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing anti-spoofing systems report either an utterance-level score or a time-based spoof interval: the former cannot show which words are spoofed, while the latter does not directly match the transcript and must be post-aligned with words, so alignment errors can lead to wrong word-level labels. Standard ASR model outputs only text; spoof information in the audio is lost after recognition and is not passed with the transcript. Yet changing only a few words can change the meaning of a sentence, leaving downstream systems to use incorrect text without knowing which words are spoofed. We therefore treat partial anti-spoofing as tagged ASR: the model transcribes speech and marks spoofed words at the same time, directly linking spoof labels to output words. We adopt the audio LLM and use ASR-Protected Subspace Gated Fusion (APSGF) to fuse spoof cues with ASR features. Spoof cues are added only outside an ASR-protected subspace, so they do not disturb recognition features. After cross-entropy training, we fine-tune the model with Reference-Anchored Policy Optimization (RAPO). Since the SFT policy is already concentrated, multiple samples from the same input tend to receive similar rewards, resulting in weak group-wise advantages. RAPO instead generates a single sample with low sampling randomness and anchors its advantage to the reward of a reference model. This allows the model to reinforce responses that outperform the reference while suppressing those that underperform it. Experiments on five datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in jointly detecting spoofed words and preserving ASR accuracy. The code is publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Xueping Zhang, Xiaoxiao Miao, Tiantian Feng, Ming Li

item.title: AudioFM: Towards General Purpose Audio Representation Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.34183v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning audio representations that effectively bridge holistic global soundscapes with fine-grained acoustic moments is a long-standing goal in self-supervised learning. Recording-level contrastive objectives encourage agreement between pooled audio representations, but do not explicitly supervise local time-frequency representations. We introduce AudioFM, a self-supervised framework that combines recording-level contrast with patch-wise masked latent discrimination. Using visible acoustic context, a student predicts representations of masked patches and identifies their corresponding full-view teacher targets among candidates from other recordings. We further incorporate weaker supervision from eligible temporal neighbors to encourage local temporal consistency. Extensive evaluations show that AudioFM achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse audio domains in linear probing, fine-tuning, and zero-shot transfer, demonstrating superior event detection, robust scene-level understanding, and strong domain generalizability.
item.dc:creator: Yamin Li, Ruidong Zhang, Anran Wang, Eduardo Fonseca, Dan Ellis, Zechen Li, Simon A. Lee, Tao Pang, Jake Garrison, Maxwell A. Xu, Yicheng Wang, Jitian Zhang, Weizhi Zhang, Haichao Zhang, Catie Chang, Xin Liu, Anupam Pathak, Daniel McDuff, Shwetak Patel, Jake Sunshine, Yuzhe Yang, Xiaoran Fan

item.title: Does Notation Matter? MusicXML Tokenisation for Symbolic Music Generation and Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2610.34247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symbolic music representations encode musical content at varying levels of completeness, from performance-oriented formats such as MIDI to fully notated scores such as MusicXML. Yet the impact of this representational richness on deep learning models remains poorly understood. While tokenisation has been extensively studied for MIDI, score-based formats have received considerably less attention, and MusicXML in particular remains largely unexplored despite being the de-facto standard for score interchange. In this paper, we introduce the first general-purpose tokenisation framework for MusicXML, and conduct a systematic empirical study to determine whether notational richness confers a measurable advantage for deep learning on symbolic music. We train 26 autoregressive and masked language models, comparing MusicXML tokenisation against MIDI and ABC-based representations, probing the effect of different tokenisation strategies within MusicXML, and testing whether music-grammar-aware tokenisation outperforms treating scores as plain text. We evaluate music understanding tasks using linear probing across composer classification, difficulty estimation, and accompaniment suggestion, and generative tasks using objective statistical metrics and a human pairwise preference study. Our results show that MusicXML-tokenised models outperform MIDI and text-based counterparts on understanding and generative tasks.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Poltronieri, Matteo Spanio, Simone Chieppa, Xavier Serra, Mart\'in Rocamora

item.title: LeanTTS: Efficient Full-Stack Bilingual TTS for Zero-Shot Cloning and Voice Customization
item.description: arXiv:2610.34408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While recent advances in text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis have substantially improved speech quality and modeling flexibility, the development of lightweight and computationally efficient systems remains comparatively underexplored. We present LeanTTS, a bilingual complete synthesis stack that supports two complementary regimes: reference-prompt zero-shot cloning for unseen speakers and token-conditioned customization for recurring voices. LeanTTS combines a compact Mandarin polyphone front end, a structurally compressed flow-matching acoustic model, and a lightweight Vocos decoder with four-step MeanFlow generation. The resulting system contains 18.9M learned parameters, 86.12% fewer than the 136.2M-parameter ZipVoice-Vocos pipeline. On Seed-TTS-Eval, its zero-shot mode obtains 2.02 CER/62.3 SIM on Mandarin and 2.32 WER/48.3 SIM on English, exposing the quality-size trade-off under aggressive compression. With token-conditioned customized voices, the same system reaches 1.57 CER/77.2 SIM on Mandarin and 1.93 WER/76.6 SIM on English, with UTMOS scores of 3.03 and 4.33, respectively. It further achieves mean/P90 CPU RTFs of 0.049/0.061, establishing a sub-20M operating point for bilingual personalization and real-time CPU deployment. Audio demos are available at https://github.com/notlu/leantts.
item.dc:creator: Yuheng Lu, Qiulin Li, Xi Wang, Yang Wang, Shengpei Jiang, Liyin Liang, Yifeng Qian, Longbiao Wang

item.title: Spatial Audio Generation and Editing with Executable Plans and Self-Distilling Transfusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.34415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial audio authoring coordinates source decisions with soundfield synthesis. For editing, plans specify what to change and retain, while reference audio supplies further acoustic detail. We present AMBIT, a unified framework for native First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) generation and editing with three connected contributions. First, a shared Transfusion backbone couples autoregressive planning with rectified-flow rendering through executable ScenePlans that specify source content, activity, and 3D trajectories. For editing, the plan describes the full target scene, including retained sources; contrastive features ground the requested change, while full reference latents supply residual acoustic detail for preservation. Second, an FOA-aware continuous VAE combines shared-decoder omnidirectional recovery, asymmetric grouped KL, and spatial covariance matching to preserve content and inter-channel structure. Third, joint Transfusion on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) refines planning on student-generated prefixes and rendering at sampling states reached under student plans, with target-conditioned teachers supervising both modes of the shared student. Evaluations across speech, music, and sound show improved generation content and spatial quality, acoustic fidelity during instruction-guided editing, and unedited-source preservation over the compared baselines. Project page: https://wjm-george.github.io/AMBIT/
item.dc:creator: Kam Man Wu, Yu Zhang, Pengjun Fang, Mingfei Chen, Weijia Chen, Zeyue Tian, Qifeng Chen

item.title: STFT Frontend Mismatch in Pretrained Audio Spectrogram Transformers: Analysis and Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained audio spectrogram transformers are widely used as backbones of machine listening systems for sound event classification. However, they are typically trained using spectrograms with a fixed Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) configuration, implicitly binding the model to the time-frequency resolution seen during pretraining. In practice, adapting these systems to new domains or computational constraints often requires different STFT frontend parameters. In this work, we conduct a controlled study of the sensitivity of the foundational Audio Spectrogram Transformer to variations in STFT window and hop size, showing that audio classification performance degrades substantially as frontend parameters deviate from pretraining settings. As a mitigation strategy, we introduce a lightweight conditioning mechanism using FiLM that enables a pretrained model to adapt to variable input configurations using limited additional training data. Our method generalizes well to unseen STFT configurations, improving model robustness without sacrificing performance in the original setting.
item.dc:creator: Julia Wilkins, Wei-Ching Lin, Abinaya Kumar, Shabnam Ghaffarzadegan, Juan Pablo Bellow

item.title: Audio-R1: Audio Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning on Self-Supervised Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2610.34609v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning is increasingly important for large audio-language models (LALMs), yet remains relatively underexplored compared with text-only and vision-language models. We introduce Audio-R1, a reinforcement learning (RL) post-training framework that revisits audio self-supervised learning as a source of verifiable rewards for improving audio understanding and reasoning task performance. Audio-R1 uses answers automatically determined during the construction of self-supervised tasks to verify model responses and compute rewards. Experiments across multiple LALMs and diverse audio benchmarks show consistent performance gains, while ablations demonstrate the benefits of each self-supervised task and additional gains from joint training. While both supervised fine-tuning and Audio-R1 improve self-supervised task accuracy, Audio-R1 further improves performance on downstream tasks distinct from the training tasks. These results highlight the potential of RL post-training with self-supervised audio tasks to improve downstream performance and reasoning-trace quality.
item.dc:creator: Jihoon Jeong, Mirco Ravanelli, Zhepei Wang, Cem Subakan

item.title: From Speech Tokens to Stolen Voices: Attacker-Chosen-Text Speaker Impersonation via Representation Inversion
item.description: arXiv:2610.34688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech interaction systems have gradually evolved from traditional cascaded systems that use text as intermediate information to end-to-end speech language models that directly process speech representations. In some applications, the speech frontend runs on the user's device and sends speech representations to a remote server for inference, while the original audio remains local. However, these representations may still contain speaker identity information. If an attacker obtains them, it may use this information to imitate the user's voice, threatening their voice privacy. To investigate this risk, we propose \stia, a Speech Token Inversion Attack that generates speech with attacker-specified text in a victim's voice using a single short leaked representation, without access to the original audio or its transcript. Specifically, \stia converts discrete, continuous, or mixed speech representations into conditioning sequences and trains a conditional flow-matching speech generation model using pairs of different utterances from the same speaker in public speech datasets. The model combines speaker characteristics contained in the leaked representation with the specified text to generate speech in the victim's voice. Experiments show that, with a Moshi representation leak corresponding to 3 seconds of speech, \stia achieves an average CAM++ speaker cosine similarity of 0.78 and a target-text word error rate of 3.80\%. These results show that speech frontend representations reveal reusable speaker identity information and highlight the need to consider privacy risks when designing speech frontend representation methods.
item.dc:creator: Ye Lu, Shen Wang, Runze Liu, Zhitao Ou, Haonan Huang, Yihan Yan, Fanghui Sun, Zhaoyang Zhang

item.title: Gangqinpu: A Multi-Genre, Multi-Task Piano Dataset with Aligned Audio, MIDI, and Musical Scores
item.description: arXiv:2610.34694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligned audio, performance MIDI, and musical scores provide valuable supervision for music analysis and performance modeling, yet datasets that jointly align all three modalities remain scarce and limited in scale and genre diversity. We introduce Gangqinpu, a multi-genre piano dataset containing 18,786 score-performance pairs and 1,007.1 hours of source audio, with automatic note-level alignments and derived beat/downbeat annotations. It spans diverse genres, including pop, classical, jazz, folk/traditional, rock, and blues. Our automated pipeline transcribes piano audio, aligns the resulting MIDI with musical scores, assigns genre labels, and filters out non-expressive performances with a score-informed binary classifier. We further construct joint splits with ASAP using conservative score-similarity grouping to reduce data leakage. We evaluate Gangqinpu on performance MIDI-to-score transcription, expressive performance rendering, and beat tracking. Downstream experiments demonstrate the value of Gangqinpu as complementary training data, with cross-dataset gains in beat tracking and primarily in-domain benefits for transcription and expressive performance rendering. The code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/wei-zeng98/gangqinpu.
item.dc:creator: Wei Zeng, Anvay Mathur, Ye Wang

item.title: S2SND-v2: Unified Online and Offline Speaker Diarization with Speaker-Adapted w2v-BERT 2.0
item.description: arXiv:2610.34707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents S2SND-v2, a unified online and offline speaker diarization framework built on S2SND that improves acoustic feature extraction and the use of the resulting representations. For acoustic feature extraction, we introduce a speaker-adapted w2v-BERT 2.0 front end and compare full and pruned construction routes. To better use these features, overlap-aware activity-query masking improves speaker embedding extraction under overlap, while late-speaker training aligns unknown-speaker training with online inference conditions. Combining these improvements, the pruned system achieves competitive average diarization error rates of 14.52% online and 12.03% offline across eight test sets.
item.dc:creator: Jincheng Wang, Li Li, Weixin Zhu, Yannan Wang, Tao Yu, Juan Liu, Ming Li

item.title: ImageTTS: Repurposing Pretrained Image Diffusion Transformers for Speech Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2610.34807v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretrained image-generation models have been successfully repurposed for various downstream visual tasks. Whether their learned representations and generative priors can transfer beyond vision to other modalities remains largely unresolved, particularly for speech synthesis, which requires linguistic fidelity and preservation of speaker identity from a short reference. We present ImageTTS, which repurposes FLUX.2 for speech synthesis by encoding pseudo-RGB log-mel spectrograms with its frozen image VAE and adapting only its pretrained Diffusion Transformer (DiT) using conditional latent flow matching. This formulation disentangles two forms of vision-to-speech transfer: representation transfer through the image VAE and generative-prior transfer through DiT initialization. The frozen image VAE largely preserves intelligibility and speaker identity with 0.99 STOI and 0.95 speaker similarity, while image-pretrained DiT initialization accelerates convergence and improves linguistic accuracy, reducing WER from 4.2\% to 2.7\% at 100k matched updates relative to random initialization. The same framework supports both zero-shot and instruction-guided TTS and, when scaled to 100K hours of speech data, achieves 1.12\% WER on Seed-TTS test-en and a Style-ACC of 0.66 on CapSpeech, outperforming speech-native baselines trained on comparable data across both tasks. These results suggest that pretrained image models can transfer beyond architectural reuse, supplying useful latent representations and generative priors for intelligible and controllable speech synthesis.
item.dc:creator: Hanchen Pei, Shujie Liu, Yayue Deng, Fangyun Wei, Yanqing Liu, Jianwei Yu, Gongping Huang

item.title: A Hierarchical Method for Environmental Sounds Recognition in Complex Acoustic Scenes
item.description: arXiv:2610.34931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Environmental noise identification is essential for noise control, yet conventional single-stage classifiers suffer from class confusion under imbalanced multiclass conditions. This paper proposes a lightweight hierarchical model integrating a Frequency-Time Adaptive Network (FTANet) with a two-stage classification mechanism. FTANet employs parallel asymmetric one-dimensional convolutions to capture temporal dynamics and frequency-band distributions, while adaptive fusion attention (AFA) enhances discriminative acoustic features. In the first stage, FTANet classifies sounds into five coarse-grained categories covering 25 fine-grained classes. In the second stage, samples are routed to the corresponding category-specific classifiers for fine-grained recognition. On a self-constructed dataset, FTANet achieves 95.45% coarse-grained accuracy with only 0.2004M parameters. On UrbanSound8K, it achieves 79.24% mean accuracy and 80.37% mean F1-score in ten-fold evaluation, outperforming compared convolutional models. Field tests on the Tianjin Online Acoustic Environment Monitoring Platform yield 87.94% coarse-grained accuracy and 97.21% conditional fine-grained accuracy for natural sounds correctly routed to C2. The complete hierarchical model achieves 87.18% overall accuracy and 87.40% weighted-average F1-score, demonstrating its feasibility for urban environmental noise monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Zhouwen Li, Haijun Lin, Bowen Lv, Yupeng Chen

item.title: The Voice on the Line
item.description: arXiv:2610.35272v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A transcriber listening through one microphone also hears everyone near it. We train causal voice isolators: masking transformers of 140M, 243M and 374M parameters, 20 ms of latency, enrolling the caller from the call itself. Short evaluation windows hide two failures that real calls expose: forgetting the caller when another voice talks alone for a while, and damaging a caller who is alone. Long calls with turns, memory beyond the attention window, real headset crosstalk and drifting caller levels address both, but each trades one against the other. WavLM-Large's own weights, made causal and trained with the model, move the trade: M with them (555M parameters) lowers the error on our development sets from 11.44% to 10.55%; a student trained from scratch to imitate WavLM does not, and w2v-BERT 2.0 and Whisper's encoder, pre-trained on far more audio, help less or not at all. A lone caller loses most at the start of a recording: no training call opened with someone already talking. Training on windows cut from longer calls lowers the error on clean development calls from 3.92% to 2.96%; this is our release. Live, the release makes 16.13% word errors on 60 s AMI windows, against 23.66% for VoxLock, the strongest open isolator, and 10.19% on its own AMI windows, against 11.71%; it is level on Krisp's benchmark (5.74% against 5.63%), and a caller who is alone still loses more words than with VoxLock (5.58% against 2.92% on clean test calls). Distilled into 22.1M parameters without WavLM, it runs live on one CPU thread inside a LiveKit agent, at 33% of a core per call in 20 ms frames, with 10.66% error on our development sets (the release 10.49%). We open-source the release and this CPU model, with a LiveKit plugin, at https://huggingface.co/collections/Scicom-intl/voice-isolator.
item.dc:creator: Husein Zolkepli

item.title: Geometric Consistency Based Label-Free Validation for Checkpoint Selection in Audio Active Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.35329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio active learning (AL) trains a classifier at low annotation cost by labeling only an informative fraction of an unlabeled collection over successive rounds. Each round picks one of the checkpoints saved during training. Mainstream AL protocols do so with an assumed validation set, but in practice its labels also count toward the annotation cost, shrinking the advantage of an already small annotation budget. We propose geometric consistency, a label-free validation rule for checkpoint selection. Both classifiers, nearest-class-mean and k-nearest-neighbor, are built from the labeled set in a frozen pretrained embedding space. They then predict the unlabeled data to model its geometry. The rule scores each checkpoint by its agreement with these pseudo-labels and its cross-entropy on the labeled set. It works with any query strategy, has one hyperparameter, insensitive in practice, and adds only one batched forward pass over the unlabeled data per round. At matched label budgets across datasets, encoders, and query strategies, it attains the best mean rank in area under the labeling curve (AULC) among methods without extra labels and is on par with an out-of-budget validation set. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of label-free validation for checkpoint selection in audio AL.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Zhang, Tuomas Virtanen

item.title: Dolphin broadband transient vocalization detection in impulsive ambient noise
item.description: arXiv:2610.35641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring in tropical waters such as those in Southeast Asia is hampered by the persistent, high-level impulsive noise of snapping shrimp. This is a particularly daunting challenge for detecting broadband transient vocalizations of dolphins - clicks, buzzes and burst-pulses. These vocalizations, unlike frequency-modulated whistles, share the broadband, impulsive character of the shrimp snaps and cannot be easily separated from them by frequency-localized or energy-based means. We develop TRIDENT, a lightweight waveform-based detector for these vocalizations, and apply it to 54.2 recorder-months of data from ten island sites around Singapore. We show that the training-data pipeline and the architecture are both important: controlled signal-to-noise-ratio based mixing to generate training data, appropriate normalization and hard negative mining, together steer the detector toward learning transient temporal structure rather than energy shortcuts. A single joint detector handles all three signal types better than specialized models for each, and outperforms established baselines. Applied to long-term recordings, it reveals tightly clustered, predominantly daytime activity, motivating days-with-detections as a robust indicator of cetacean presence.
item.dc:creator: Hari Vishnu, Jin Xinhui, Mandar Chitre, Simen Hexeberg, Koay Teong Beng

item.title: Graph Neural Network for Wide-Area 6DoF Ambisonic Rendering
item.description: arXiv:2610.35741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wide-area 6DoF rendering from sparse Ambisonic recordings is commonly addressed by interpolating parametric spatial descriptors rather than the waveforms themselves. This preserves the fidelity of a nearby measured signal and avoids phase artifacts caused by mixing distant arrays. However, existing DirAC-based approaches rely on geometric interpolation weights that do not depend on the acoustic scene observed by the microphones. We propose a lightweight Graph Neural Network (GNN) that refines only this interpolation stage. The known Ambisonic arrays and the query position are represented as a graph whose nodes contain local DirAC features and whose edges encode relative distance and directional relations. The network predicts positive query-conditioned weights over the measured arrays, while the target energy, diffuseness, and direction of arrival are reconstructed by an analytical DirAC layer. Experiments on unseen rooms, unseen speech signals, and unseen array configurations show that the proposed weighting improves energy reconstruction and radiation-pattern similarity with respect to baseline interpolation.
item.dc:creator: Gioele Greco, Filippo Marri, Mirco Pezzoli, Fabio Antonacci

item.title: Correspondence Is Not Transfer: A Pairing-Controlled Audit of Clinical Audio-Metadata Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.35747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical audio models increasingly align recordings with participant metadata or metadata-derived text. This supervision is useful but ambiguous: the paired target can contain symptoms, demographics, missingness, and cohort structure, not just disease information. We study this ambiguity by making the audio-metadata pairing itself the intervention. Our Pairing-Controlled Transfer Audit trains matched contrastive trajectories under correct pairing, global shuffling, disease-label-preserving shuffling, and label-and-recorded-sex-preserving shuffling. Each endpoint is then frozen and tested with three readouts: profile correspondence, attribute decodability, and matched disease prediction. On UKCOVID, correct improves retrieval and sex decodability over label-only shuffling, showing that the pairing intervention worked. The sex-probe contrast is largely absorbed by the sex-preserving control, while smaller retrieval differences remain. Disease-transfer contrasts, however, remain uncertain. After UKCOVID discovery fixed the pipeline, CODA TB, Cambridge COVID-19 Sounds, and Coswara were rerun as a locked external panel with the same arms, backbones, matching, readout, calibration, primary contrast, and primary metric. The external panel preserves the descriptive separation without proving a universal null. Successful profile correspondence and improved disease transfer are therefore different empirical claims.
item.dc:creator: Liu He, Xi Wang, Jiahong Yuan, Yuanchao Li

item.title: Feature Scaling Beats Architecture Choice in Offline Respiratory Screening for Low-Resource Clinics
item.description: arXiv:2610.33030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep models are the usual choice for respiratory sound classification, but in clinics without GPUs or connectivity that choice carries a cost. We compare classical and deep classifiers on a five-class respiratory-sound corpus of 1,211 clips (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, Bronchial, healthy) from 201 patient groups, with a 3.86:1 class imbalance, using pre-registered patient-grouped cross-validation (25 runs per configuration). An SVM over 30 summary features (MFCC, ZCR and RMS statistics) reaches macro recall 0.78 and 0.71 recall on the rarest class. A 1.13M-parameter convolutional recurrent network over log-Mel spectrograms reaches 0.75 to 0.77, and no difference between model families is resolved. The largest single effect we measure is a preprocessing effect rather than an architectural one. Standardizing the SVM's features, a routine step for RBF kernels, moves its macro recall from 0.51 to 0.78, a 27-point swing wider than any gap between model families here. Augmentation did not help: SMOTE, waveform augmentation and SpecAugment have no measurable effect. Latency does not separate the models (51 to 74 ms per clip on a CPU-only laptop), but the classical models avoid a 449 MB PyTorch runtime. Clip-level splits, which let a patient's recordings fall on both sides, inflate macro recall by 7.5 to 9.8 points. Recording source is strongly tied to label (Cramer's V = 0.65 between native sampling rate and class), and in an exploratory analysis clips recorded at a class's minority rate are mostly assigned to classes typical of that rate; we state this confound as the paper's main limitation.
item.dc:creator: Abubakar Chilala, Cleophas Kadima, Innocent Anyaele, Victor Olufemi

item.title: A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.33036v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
item.dc:creator: Shreeram Suresh Chandra, Ashwyn Sharma, Liang Lu, Xiutian Zhao, Leda Sari, Bj\"orn Schuller, Berrak Sisman

item.title: Support-guided OOD Removal with Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.33194v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many real-world signals are corrupted by localized, structured perturbations whose distribution is unknown: an intermittent background noise in a music recording, a watermark stamped on a photograph, a cast shadow. We study the task of recovering a clean signal $x$ from an observation $y$ containing such a localized out-of-distribution (OOD) corruption. We propose Support-guided OOD Removal with Diffusion, SORD, an iterative algorithm to recover $x$ using only two ingredients: a binary map of the corruption support and a single diffusion model pretrained on clean signals. SORD does not require any paired data or any statistical model of the corruption. We evaluate SORD on natural images and human faces with spatially localized corruptions including handwritten digits, other images, watermarks, and shadows, as well as audio recordings of different musical instruments with temporally localized corruptions including other instruments and human speech. SORD is competitive with, and often outperforms, posterior-sampling inpainting given the same diffusion prior and the same mask, source-separation baselines that require a separate diffusion model for each source, and, on several benchmarks, supervised networks trained on paired clean and corrupted signals. The code is released here: \href{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}{https://github.com/voilalab/SORD}.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Kheirandish, Sara Fridovich-Keil

item.title: AV-QTSS: Class-Query Target Sound Spatialization in Multi-Source 360$^\circ$ Videos
item.description: arXiv:2610.34401v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial audio is central to immersive 360$^\circ$ media, yet existing audio-visual spatialization renders the scene as a whole, leaving no control over an individual source. We introduce Audio-Visual Query-conditioned Target Sound Spatialization (AV-QTSS): given a monaural multi-source mixture, a 360$^\circ$ video and a class query from the 13-class DCASE sound-event ontology, it generates the first-order Ambisonics (FOA) signal of the queried source alone. The omnidirectional mixture contains no explicit spatial cues, so direction has to be inferred from the video, where several objects may sound at once. We propose a query-conditioned dense binding localizer that predicts a spherical probability map over the whole scene, coupled to the renderer so both are optimized jointly. Experiments with one to four concurrent sources show improved localization and spatial accuracy relative to established methods and ablated variants, and the localizer transfers to real 360$^\circ$ recordings after adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Qingyu Luo, Peng Zhang, Wenwu Wang, Philip J. B. Jackson

item.title: In-Context Adapter Generation for Compositional Generalization in Large Audio Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.34413v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) have achieved strong performance on standard speech and audio understanding tasks, yet their ability to systematically generalize to novel task compositions remains underexplored. Taking a meta-learning view, we extend Text-to-LoRA (T2L) to LALMs, generating instruction-conditioned LoRA adapters with a Transformer hypernetwork rather than learning a single fixed adapter shared across instructions. To exploit fine-grained task information, we introduce in-context adapter generation (ICAG), a token-level hypernetwork architecture; we call the resulting method T2L-ICAG. We evaluate this approach on two representative LALMs using SIFT-50M for supervised fine-tuning and construct a controlled compositional evaluation suite covering five task classes. Across two LALM backbones, T2L-ICAG consistently improves over static LoRA and also the global embedding-based T2L baseline. Coverage and capacity analyses further show that these gains are larger on structurally out-of-domain tasks and cannot be explained by parameter count alone. These results suggest that generating task-specific adapters from instructions is a promising direction for improving compositional generalization of LALMs.
item.dc:creator: Yiwei Guo, Siqi Huang, Bohan Li, Jing Peng, Hankun Wang, Zhihan Li, Kai Yu

item.title: Finite-Sample Sensitivity of Kernel Metrics for Generative Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kernel distances such as the Kernel Inception Distance (KID) and the Kernel Audio Distance (KAD) compare generated and reference samples in an embedding space, and model comparisons rest on their values. Each ships with one fixed kernel, and a reported value does not say which changes that kernel detects at the sample size used. We run each default as a permutation two-sample test on real embeddings of symbolic music, audio and images, comparing a sample with an independent sample changed by a mean shift, an isotropic contraction, or a rotation that keeps the mean and the covariance trace and is matched to the shift in transport distance. At 780 samples per side, both defaults rarely detect the rotations in five evaluation spaces, while they detect the shifts in every run. The median-bandwidth Gaussian kernel of KAD detects the contraction and regains power against rotations on image embeddings with an order of magnitude more samples. The cubic kernel of KID contains second- and third-moment information but misses the contraction in most runs, and our experiments do not establish a high-power rotation regime for it over the tested sample sizes. Narrower Gaussian bandwidths restore sensitivity in music and audio, an $\ell_1$ Laplace kernel does so for images, and aggregated tests combine both at nominal level. We recommend that a reported kernel distance state its sample budget and the changes its configuration detects at that budget.
item.dc:creator: Tomasz Radzikowski, Mateusz Modrzejewski

item.title: When the Persona Contradicts the Line: Diagnosing Plan-to-Synthesis Failures in Chain-of-Thought TTS
item.description: arXiv:2610.35008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought TTS systems rely on language-model planners to translate persona and context into vocal delivery, but it is unclear where this intent is lost when the requested affect conflicts with lexical sentiment. We introduce a bilingual Japanese--English persona--line conflict benchmark in which each item pairs one line with congruent and conflicting personas and pre-declares the expected acoustic direction. We probe this direction in the planner-generated delivery phrase, the planner-written emotion vector, the QwenEmotion-generated vector, and the rendered waveform. Planner outputs are usually direction-correct, while downstream agreement can be substantially lower. Bypassing QwenEmotion provides only modest gains over the full planner-controlled Base. Supervising QwenEmotion raises the direction rate to 75% in Japanese and 84% in English. A learned text-to-latent interface reaches the highest English rate of 89% and the highest Japanese arousal rate of 88%. These results show that learned repair of the plan-to-synthesis interface can recover counter-textual delivery, although its effect differs across languages and acoustic axes.
item.dc:creator: Joonyong Park, Jerry Li

item.title: Should Pseudo-Labels Share Mini-Batches with Labeled Examples? Semi-Supervised Continual Active Learning with Limited Training Cost
item.description: arXiv:2610.35345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Active learning (AL) reduces annotation by querying informative examples. Continual active learning (CAL) also cuts the training cost, the total number of gradient steps, by training one model across AL rounds with a fixed number of mini-batch steps per round. Pseudo-labels add supervision without annotation, but they increase training cost. In CAL, where every round trains on a fixed number of mini-batches, whether and how pseudo-labeled examples should share these mini-batches with labeled examples is therefore open. We provide the first formalization of this problem as two decisions after each query, namely (i) which unlabeled examples should enter training with a pseudo-label and (ii) what share of each mini-batch they should take. Our method, semi-supervised continual active learning (SSCAL), works with any acquisition function. It admits pseudo-labels based on distances from unlabeled examples to labeled neighbors, caps their share, and reweights the loss on labeled examples to keep their expected gradient contribution unchanged. On frozen embeddings, its pseudo-labeler updates incrementally without extra model forward passes. Across two audio datasets, two frozen encoders, six acquisition functions and ten seeds, SSCAL ranks first on average among four protocols with equal training steps, answering the question affirmatively.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Zhang, Tuomas Virtanen

item.title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.35581v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A full-duplex spoken dialogue model must yield when the user cuts in and hold when the user merely backchannels. Sequence-level RL with a timing reward (GRPO) is the usual recipe; we test its whole-rollout form on four open models and find two failures. A binary window reward gives zero advantage on exactly the windows that most need learning (a zero-gradient trap), and the one score per rollout is spread over listening-state decisions the reward is not written in terms of (credit leakage), so the model talks into silence or stops answering. Both come from sampling a reward that is a known function of a few binary control decisions. We propose \emph{window likelihood} (\WL): sample a continuation per window, but integrate in closed form over the stop decisions it visits and maximise the log-probability of acting correctly---a noisy-OR for yielding, a survival product for holding. On HumDial-FDBench, \WL\ gives the best yield/hold F1 on all six structurally different open models we post-train, exceeds Kyutai's released GRPO checkpoints (trained on different data), and adds no re-opening of the floor on any model.
item.dc:creator: Guoqiang Hu, Lichao Zhang, Yizhou Peng, Yuhao Luo, Haifeng Hu, Sallen Sun, Will Yang, Eng Siong Chng

item.title: Multimodal Concert Video Editing: System Design and Exploratory Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35816v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Editing multi-camera concerts requires coordinated decisions about musical relevance, visual quality and cut timing. We present a modular framework that combines instrument activity from multitrack audio, visible instruments and image sharpness with beat-based timing and probabilistic camera selection. An interpretable scoring model links these components to the choice of views over complete shot intervals. Component tests and an exploratory expert study on a four-camera concert yield mixed assessments across the editing variants. The findings motivate extending local audiovisual relevance with contextual and sequence-level criteria. The architecture provides a basis for testing these extensions and studying how component behaviour affects the quality of complete edits.
item.dc:creator: Lennart Schiweck, Adrian Kempf, Michelle Retig, Moritz Feucht, Tim Mangliers, Benjamin Himpel

item.title: The Affective Bridge: Preserving Speech Representations while Enhancing Deepfake Detection via emotional Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2512.11241v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speech deepfake detection (DFD) has benefited from diverse acoustic and semantic speech representations, many of which encode valuable speech information and are costly to train. Prior work has shown that affective cues improve DFD, yet existing approaches either fuse emotion with other task-specific features in complex pipelines or directly fine-tune representations toward DFD objectives, risking distortion of the original speech representations that support downstream tasks such as speaker verification (SV) or automatic speech recognition (ASR). We propose a simpler approach: fine-tuning speech encoders on emotion recognition alone-without any DFD supervision, and training a lightweight support vector machine (SVM) on the frozen emotion-tuned representations for DFD. This preserves the original representation capacity for downstream tasks such as SV and ASR, while emergently improving DFD performance. Crucially, we find that emotion is uniquely effective as this bridging task: replacing it with speaker identity even degrades DFD performance, demonstrating that the benefit stems from emotion's role as a natural bridge between speech representation and DFD. Experiments on FakeOrReal and In-the-Wild show accuracy improvements of up to 6\% and 2\% with corresponding EER reductions, while analysis on ASVspoof 2019 LA reveals dataset-specific speaker bias in the real-speech subset. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/myxp-lyp/The-Affective-Bridge-Unifying-Feature-Representations-for-Speech-Deepfake-Detection}{GitHub repository}.
item.dc:creator: Yupei Li, Chenyang Lyu, Longyue Wang, Weihua Luo, Kaifu Zhang, Bj\"orn W. Schuller

item.title: Do Compact SSL Backbones Matter for Audio Deepfake Detection? A Controlled Study with RAPTOR
item.description: arXiv:2603.06164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) underpins modern audio deepfake detection, yet most prior work centers on a single large wav2vec2-XLSR backbone, leaving compact under studied. We present RAPTOR, Representation Aware Pairwise-gated Transformer for Out-of-domain Recognition a controlled study of compact SSL backbones from the HuBERT and WavLM within a unified pairwise-gated fusion detector, evaluated across 14 cross-domain benchmarks. We show that multilingual HuBERT pre-training is the primary driver of cross-domain robustness, enabling 100M models to match larger and commercial systems. Beyond EER, we introduce a test-time augmentation protocol with perturbation-based aleatoric uncertainty to expose calibration differences invisible to standard metrics: WavLM variants exhibit overconfident miscalibration under perturbation, whereas iterative mHuBERT remains stable. These findings indicate that SSL pre-training trajectory, not model scale, drives reliable audio deepfake detection.
item.dc:creator: Ajinkya Kulkarni, Sandipana Dowerah, Atharva Kulkarni, Tanel Alum\"ae, Mathew Magimai Doss

item.title: Building a Dataset for Music Sample Identification
item.description: arXiv:2609.15465v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sample identification (SI) is the task of matching an element of a musical work to its musically transformed versions used to create new works. The task has received little attention and lacks large-scale publicly available data. In this work, we mine sampling annotations from a music database and split them for training and evaluation. The resulting dataset is nearly three orders of magnitude larger than the existing SI benchmarks, with training, validation, and test sets of 114 k, 6 k, and 10 k tracks. We find that naively splitting the annotations places the same tracks in different sets. To avoid this, we construct a graph from the annotations and split it over connected components. We further find that a single mega-component contains half of the annotations, making component-wise splitting incompatible with balanced splits; we trim it, yielding a leakage-aware pipeline. We share the dataset for non-commercial scientific research purposes only and make the data-analysis and splitting code publicly available. We hope that our work fosters research on SI.
item.dc:creator: R. Oguz Araz, Xavier Lizarraga, Xavier Serra, Dmitry Bogdanov

item.title: Structure Across Voices: Comparing acoustic-event type accumulation and sequence dependence across four vocal corpora using frozen audio encoders
item.description: arXiv:2609.16612v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Comparing acoustic structure across very different vocal corpora is difficult because the recordings use different native event units, contain different amounts of sequence, and were collected under different conditions. We develop a matched procedure for comparing such corpora without forcing them into the same event definition. Frozen audio encoders provide a common acoustic representation for recorded events, while matched sampling gives each corpus the same amount of evidence for acoustic and sequence analysis. We apply this procedure to sperm-whale codas, human speech phones, Bengalese-finch syllables, and common-marmoset calls. The comparison reveals different patterns across the four corpora. Sperm-whale recordings stand out broadly: new acoustic forms continue to appear, while their sequences also show strong organization and repetition. Finch recordings show the strongest organization of sounds over time, especially in how neighboring sounds and repeated patterns are arranged. Direct temporal and spectral measurements show that these differences are also present in the recorded sounds themselves. The comparison provides a practical way to measure acoustic diversity and temporal organization across very different vocal corpora by combining a common acoustic representation with matched observation opportunity, without treating their native sounds as equivalent.
item.dc:creator: Mudit Sinha, Sanika Chavan

item.title: RMS-AQA: A Two-Stage Spatial Audio Question Answering Benchmark for Real-World Domestic Environments
item.description: arXiv:2610.00935v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Embodied assistants in domestic environments must infer what happened, where and when it occurred, and how to respond. To address this, we introduce RMS-AQA, a spatial audio question answering (SAQA) benchmark for real-world domestic environments. The benchmark features a two-stage question-answering (QA) format to comprehensively assess the ability of audio-language models (ALMs) to first ground audible sound events and subsequently perform complex spatio-temporal reasoning based on that grounding. To maximize acoustic realism, our dataset combines authentic real-world first-order Ambisonics (FOA) recordings with high-fidelity synthetic data generated using measured room impulse responses (RIRs). Furthermore, we provide a lightweight spatial plug-in that injects FOA-format data into frozen audio-language backbones. Experimental results reveal that the primary challenges stem from concurrent sources, far distance, and sim-to-real domain gap between RIR-synthesized and authentic recordings.
item.dc:creator: Peihao Chen, Qing Wang, Lichun Fan, Yufeng Hao, Zhifeng Kong, Mengyao Zhu, Hengyi Hong, Hang Chen, Hang Su, Yujie Jian, Chao-Han Huck Yang, Shichao Hu, Jun Du, Jian Luan, Ke Li

item.title: Commanding at the Speed of Sound: Audio-Centric Referring Expression Segmentation for Aerial Scenes
item.description: arXiv:2610.26872v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Referring expression segmentation (RES) aims to localize targets at the pixel level guided by human instructions. However, current models predominantly follow a text-centric paradigm that treats discrete text as the primary interaction medium for these human instructions. This assumption is especially limiting in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, where rapid response, hands-free operation, and natural communication are often critical. In this paper, we reconstruct UAV referring expression segmentation through an audio-centric perspective. Grounded in information theory, we demonstrate that raw audio provides a higher upper bound for extracting rich semantic features than transcribed text. To achieve this, we construct an audio-driven UAV referring expression segmentation benchmark named Aerial-AudioRES by augmenting VisDrone with synthesized speech, forming "audio-text-image-mask" quadruples. Specifically, we employ an ambiguity filtering mechanism to ensure referential uniqueness, and incorporate eight distinct timbres alongside 4 realistic noises to simulate authentic environments. To drive the paradigm shift from text-centric to audio-centric, we propose the end-to-end Audio-centric Referring Expression Segmentation Network (ARES-Net). Distinct from discrete text-visual matching, our approach learns to establish a direct soft alignment between continuous acoustic manifolds and multi-scale visual representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our method obtains a peak accuracy of 64.23% in oIoU and demonstrates robust generalization on a collected real-human test set. Furthermore, it significantly reduces total interaction latency to one-third of the text-based method. Our code is available at https://github.com/LemonGauss/ARES-Net.
item.dc:creator: Ziyun Chen, Yijun Wang, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuexuan An, Xiang Gu, Wei Zhou, Fan Liu

item.title: Encode Once, Decode Never: Reusing Audio LM Internals for Efficient Temporal Localization
item.description: arXiv:2602.10230v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Audio language models process input audio into rich frame-level representations, but the standard approach to temporal localization generates timestamps as sequences of text tokens, which discards the frame-level representations in favor of autoregressive decoding. However, generating timestamps as tokens is slow and not parallelizable, and tends to hallucinate when producing timestamps outside the training distribution. We propose internal frame-level reuse, a method that trains audio LMs to reuse their own internal audio representations for temporal localization directly, bypassing token generation altogether. We introduce a lightweight prediction head trained via different frame-level objectives: a binary frame classifier and a novel inhomogeneous Poisson process (IHP) loss that models temporal event intensity. Across word localization, speaker diarization, and event localization tasks, our approach can achieve a >50x inference speedup over token-based generation and demonstrates robust length generalization, maintaining high accuracy on out-of-distribution audio durations where token-based models collapse completely. We find that reusing audio frame-level representations yields localization accuracies comparable to (and often better than) finetuned token-based baselines.
item.dc:creator: Joseph An, Phillip Keung, Jiaqi Wang, Orevaoghene Ahia, Noah A. Smith

item.title: SLT 2026 REAL-TSE Challenge: Real-world Target Speaker Extraction from Conversational Recordings
item.description: arXiv:2607.15198v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce the REAL-TSE Challenge, an IEEE SLT 2026 satellite challenge on target speaker extraction~(TSE) from real conversational recordings. Given a multi-speaker mixture and one or more enrollment utterances from a target speaker, participating systems must recover only the target speech. Unlike simulated read-speech benchmarks, REAL-TSE evaluates Mandarin and English recordings that contain natural overlap, reverberation, noise, channel mismatch, and conversational dynamics. The challenge defines two complementary tracks: an Online track for low-latency streaming extraction and an Offline track for full-context processing. Systems are evaluated with Token Error Rate (TER), Speaker Similarity (SpkSim), DNSMOS, and target-speaker activity F1. This overview paper describes the task definition, datasets, baselines, evaluation protocol, submitted systems, condition-wise findings, and lessons for future real-world TSE benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Shuai Wang, Zihan Qian, Ke Zhang, Jiangyu Han, Zikai Liu, Xiaoyang Yu, Haoyu Li, Marc Delcroix, Kai Yu, Lei Xie, Ming Li, Haizhou Li

item.title: The Machines Are Calling: Measuring Automated and Synthetic Voices in Unwanted Inbound Calls
item.description: arXiv:2609.11137v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In February 2024 the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) placed AI-generated voices under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA). Yet no peer-reviewed measurement says how much unwanted call traffic is placed by a machine, or how much of that machine speech is synthesized rather than played from a recording. We report both with a disclosed pipeline. An interactive voice honeypot (language-model personas on real U.S. numbers, the caller recorded on its own track) recorded 10,987 calls over 66 days. Three instruments read each opening: an audio fingerprint that finds the same recording played on other calls, a commercial synthetic-speech detector on the caller's first ten seconds, and blinded listeners who check what it flags. Of the 7,233 greeted calls we analyze, 13.8% open with a recording we also heard on another call, and 13.1% with fresh audio the detector labels synthetic. A further 9.9% open with a caller who never spoke after our greeting, 54.2% with fresh audio the detector labels human, and 9.0% could not be scored. Machine-voiced openings are therefore at least 26.9%, a further tenth of calls are silent connections we read as machine-placed, and replays of a recording make up 45% of the detector's own rate (29.3% of 6,192 scored openings). The same waveform played on two calls lands on opposite sides of the detector's threshold 13.6% of the time, and eleven listeners confirm 54.4% of what it flags. Synthetic openings concentrate in lead-generation spam (33.8%), not fraud (21.1%); 0.44% disclose automation. Prevalence tracks how long a bait number has circulated (59% against 19% in the same weeks): seeding history, not calendar time, explains the trend. Campaigns outlast their numbers: one recorded compliance notice opens calls in six campaigns, and one synthetic voice serves nine.
item.dc:creator: Xingyu Shen, Tommy Duong, Muduo Xu, Xiaodong An, Jiaqi Gan, Haoyuan Tang, Jamey Z. Liang, Siyu Zhang, Yan Zhang, Ethan Traister, Simiao Ren

item.title: AV-GRPO: Modality-Anchored Decoupling Diffusion Reinforcement Learning for Joint Audio-Video Generation
item.description: arXiv:2609.29816v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent years have witnessed major progress in joint audio-video generation. Existing models still suffer from limited per-modality fidelity, insufficient text-modality alignment and weak cross-modal synchronization. While reinforcement-learning post-training offers a promising remedy, directly adapting it to joint audio-video generation is challenging. Heterogeneous multimodal rewards entangle learning signals and complicate credit assignment. Joint optimization of two modality towers is computationally expensive given their divergent dynamics. Moreover, synchronization evaluation difficulty depends on paired samples, preventing fair reward comparisons. We propose AV-GRPO, a modality-anchored online diffusion RL framework, and 5DAV, a decoupled, difficulty-controllable training dataset. AV-GRPO includes three key modules: (1) modality-anchored rollouts to disentangle learning signals and stabilize difficulty; (2) trajectory-locked frozen-tower optimization to reduce cost and reassign credit; (3) adaptive objectives and perturbation strengths tailored to modality-specific dynamics. This converts coupled multimodal preference learning into unimodal subproblems for precise reward attribution and better synchronization. Our 5DAV dataset decouples samples across five dimensions for systematic training. Experiments on JavisBench and VABench demonstrate AV-GRPO outperforms LTX-2.3 in generation quality, semantic alignment and cross-modal synchronization under LoRA and full fine-tuning. Ablations confirm our designs. Code and data: https://github.com/zhiyuxu03/AV-GRPO
item.dc:creator: Zhiyu Xu, Weilong Yan, Yufei Shi, Shiyang Li, Yihao Liu, Kin-Man Lam, Yuewen Cao

item.title: Beyond Perturbation Magnitude: Direction-Dependent Responses in Multimodal Geometric Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.08533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Geometric alignment scores based on Gram determinants provide a compact way to model higher-order consistency among modalities, yet how such scores respond to modality degradation is poorly understood. This paper asks whether the response of a multimodal geometric score is determined primarily by the magnitude of the perturbation-induced displacement. Using frozen cohorts from MSR-VTT (N=878) and DiDeMo (N=980), we apply controlled video blur and audio noise and analyze the response in the relational geometry on which the score is defined. Displacement magnitude explains at most 15% of the out-of-sample variance in the absolute response, and magnitude-matched pairs respond systematically differently, so scalar magnitude does not organize the response. The closed-form first-order expansion of the Gramian volume yields the Directional Geometric Response (DGR): the projection of the displacement onto the local volume gradient, which jointly captures the clean operating point, displacement magnitude, and displacement direction. The absolute first-order DGR term explains the observed response with out-of-sample R^2 of 0.838-0.969, matched-magnitude ranking accuracies of 0.864-0.963, and response-sign accuracies of 0.909-0.989, whereas the tested direction-free alternatives remain weak or unstable under the corresponding evaluation protocols. A pre-specified gain-normalization candidate, V/(g_V+eps), fails its predictability and clean-order gates. DGR uses the observed degraded-state displacement and is therefore an explanatory quantity, not a deployment-time predictor: geometric response depends on where the representation operates, how far degradation moves the relational geometry, and in which direction it moves.

item.title: Expert L2 English Speech Evaluation on a Gaming PC: Accuracy, Fluency, and Prosody with XLS-R, XEUS, and PhoneticXeus
item.description: arXiv:2610.26406v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: oollim is a locally executable system for evaluating L2 English pronunciation accuracy, fluency, and prosody on a consumer computer. The system combines pretrained XLS-R, XEUS, and PhoneticXeus representations with reference-text features and ridge regressions trained on SpeechOcean762, the Korean Learners' L2 Speech Corpus (English), J-AESOP, and their combinations. On 305 independently held-out recordings assessed by three expert raters, several ridge configurations substantially outperform archival Microsoft Azure Pronunciation Assessment API data in both Spearman correlation and quadratic weighted kappa across all three constructs. These results support expert speech evaluation on consumer hardware using pretrained representations and construct-specific regressions, without neural-model fine-tuning or calibration on the private evaluation data.
